Today they build the historical and cultural context of ancient Greece using words alone, with no images, so they must picture the world from text.","enduringUnderstanding":"Myths grow out of the needs, fears, and questions of the cultures that tell them, and the facts of a people's daily life help explain the stories they create.","futureLessons":"In Lesson 3, students will read Rick Riordan on adapting myths and consider what he believes myths do for people. Today's predictions will help them judge why old stories still matter to modern readers and to The Lightning Thief.","performanceTask":"In Shared Stories, Shared Lessons, students will compare texts, analyze cultural values, and use evidence from multiple sources. Today they practice gathering facts from different texts and comparing how sources present the same world."},"vocabulary":[{"word":"myth","definition":"a traditional story that explains something about the world, such as nature, human behavior, or beliefs about gods","tier":"support"},{"word":"philosophy","definition":"the study of big questions about life, truth, and how people should live","tier":"support"},{"word":"city-state","definition":"a city that governs itself and the land around it as its own small country","tier":"support"},{"word":"context clue","definition":"a hint in the words and sentences around an unfamiliar word that helps show its meaning","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"predict","definition":"to use evidence and what you know to say what is likely to happen or be true","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"prosody","definition":"the rhythm, pausing, emphasis, and tone of a voice when reading aloud","tier":"addressed"}],"texts":[{"title":"A Short History of Greek and Roman Myth","author":"Newsela","pages":"Teacher-selected paragraphs"},{"title":"Ancient Greece: The First Greeks","author":"Newsela","pages":"Teacher-selected paragraphs"},{"title":"Ancient Greek Thinkers, Truth Seekers","author":"Newsela","pages":"Teacher-selected paragraphs"}]},"sections":[{"kind":"launch","title":"Launch","purpose":"Students recall Lesson 1 ideas about why cultures create myths, practice reading aloud with prosody, and learn to use context clues so they are ready to read about ancient Greece.","activities":[{"id":"launch-recall-turn-and-talk","title":"Why Do We Need Stories?","minutes":6,"standards":["SL.6.1"],"routine":"Turn and Talk","blocks":[{"type":"directions","text":"Use the **Turn and Talk** routine. Look back at your notes from Lesson 1. Tell your partner one thing a culture might use a myth to explain."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"Yesterday we learned that myths are stories cultures tell to explain things. Today we find out what kind of world those stories came from. We will use words only, with no pictures."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What problems or mysteries might people try to explain with a story?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"They might explain things like storms, why people get sick, or where fire came from, because they didn't have science to explain them."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Why would a story be more helpful than no answer at all?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"A story makes a scary thing feel less random. It also gives people a way to share ideas and teach lessons."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"note","text":"Keep this to about six minutes. Take two or three shares and listen for references to Lesson 1 ideas such as danger, nature, and the unknown."}]},{"id":"launch-context-clues-prosody","title":"Context Clues and Reading Aloud","minutes":9,"standards":["L.6.4.a"],"routine":"Teacher Modeling","blocks":[{"type":"directions","text":"Listen as your teacher reads a sentence aloud. Then use the words around the underlined word to figure out what it means."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"A context clue is a hint in the words around a new word. I will read a sentence: 'The Greeks lived in city-states, small cities that each ruled themselves, so Athens and Sparta had different laws.' Listen to how I pause after the comma. That pause tells you a definition is coming."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What does city-state mean, and which words helped you?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"A city-state is a city that rules itself. The words 'small cities that each ruled themselves' and 'different laws' helped me."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"Prosody means reading with natural pauses, emphasis, and tone. Pauses show the reader where ideas begin and end. Today when you read aloud, pause where the meaning calls for it, and later we will ask why the author put a pause there."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"tip","text":"Write the sentence on the board and mark the comma with a slash so students can see the pause. Teach the words *philosophy* and *myth* only if they arise in context during the lesson."},{"type":"paragraph","audience":"teacher","text":"Connection to today: Students will read excerpts without images, so context clues and careful reading must carry their understanding."}]}]},{"kind":"learning-in-action","title":"Learning in Action","purpose":"Part A: Students read assigned excerpts aloud in small groups, extract facts and cite evidence, and use context clues for unfamiliar words (L.6.4.a, RI.6.1). Part B: Students predict what myths from this world would explain, make prediction posters, and compare across texts (RI.6.7, RI.6.9).","activities":[{"id":"lia-read-and-extract","title":"Part A: Reading Ancient Greece in Words Only","minutes":15,"standards":["RI.6.1","L.6.4.a","SL.6.1"],"routine":"Annotation","blocks":[{"type":"text-reference","title":"A Short History of Greek and Roman Myth; Ancient Greece: The First Greeks; Ancient Greek Thinkers, Truth Seekers","pages":"One teacher-selected paragraph group per text (about 2-3 short paragraphs each)"},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"note","text":"Prep: before class, choose short paragraphs from each article and assign one text to each group, with at least one group per article. Pick paragraphs that mention daily life, beliefs about gods, learning, farming or sea travel, or natural dangers. Use passages with a likely context-clue word such as *philosophy*, *city-state*, or *mythology*. Hand out text only, with no images."},{"type":"directions","text":"In your group, read your excerpt aloud, taking turns by sentence. Pause where the meaning calls for it. Then annotate: underline 3-4 facts about ancient Greek life, beliefs, learning, or daily challenges. Circle one word you did not know and use the surrounding words to write its meaning in the margin. Record each fact on your organizer with the sentence that proves it."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"You are only getting words today. Treat the text like a window and look closely at every detail it gives you about this world."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"After a group reads aloud: Why did the author pause here, and what idea is emphasized?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"The author used a comma before 'which' to pause, and that pause puts the focus on the idea that Greeks explained storms with gods. That is the important idea in the sentence."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What fact did you find, and which words in the text prove it?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Fact: Greeks believed gods controlled the sea. Evidence: the text says sailors prayed to Poseidon before a voyage, so it shows they depended on the sea and feared it."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What did you decide your circled word means, and how?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"I think philosophy means studying big questions, because the sentence says thinkers asked why the world works the way it does."},{"type":"pulse-check","standards":["RI.6.1"],"stem":"Which statement shows the best use of text evidence to support a fact about ancient Greek life?","choices":[{"text":"Greeks were smart because I learned that in school.","correct":false,"rationale":"This relies on outside knowledge and gives no words from the text."},{"text":"Greeks believed gods controlled nature, because the text says sailors prayed to Poseidon before a voyage.","correct":true,"rationale":"It states a fact and supports it with a detail the text provides."},{"text":"Greece had lots of islands, so everyone there was a sailor.","correct":false,"rationale":"This overgeneralizes and goes beyond what the text says."},{"text":"The text is about Greece, so it must be about gods.","correct":false,"rationale":"This is a vague guess with no specific evidence from the paragraph."}]},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Help students read closely and use accurate verbs to report facts and evidence from a text, with partner support for turn-taking.","sayAsk":"Model: 'The text says ___.' 'This shows that ___.' 'The author explains ___.' Encourage present-tense reporting verbs (says, shows, explains, suggests). Let students read the sentence chorally with a partner before reading it alone. Frame context clues: 'I think ___ means ___ because the text says ___.'","watchFor":"If students copy whole sentences without choosing a fact, then prompt: 'Say it in your own words in one short sentence.' If students use past tense for text claims ('the author said'), then model present tense: 'The author says.' Success: students state a fact and point to specific words as evidence using a reporting verb."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: finding facts in dense text","tryThis":"Assign a single paragraph and ask them to find one fact per sentence. Give a sentence starter: 'The text tells me Greeks ___.'"},{"situation":"Ready for extension: using evidence","tryThis":"Ask students to find a detail that is inferred rather than stated, and to explain which clues led them to it."}]}]},{"id":"lia-predict-posters","title":"Part B: Prediction Posters and Cross-Text Comparison","minutes":15,"standards":["RI.6.9","RI.6.7","RI.6.1","SL.6.1"],"routine":"Gallery Walk","blocks":[{"type":"directions","text":"With your group, make a prediction poster. Write your 3-4 facts on the left. On the right, answer: How might stories from a world like this sound? What fears, natural events, or mysteries would people try to explain? Cite the text for at least one prediction. Then post your poster and visit two other groups with different texts."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"A prediction is more than a guess. It is based on facts. Connect each prediction to a fact, using the frame: 'Because the text says ___, I predict myths from this world would explain ___.'"},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What fears, natural events, or mysteries might people in this world try to explain?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Because the text says Greek cities depended on the sea and farming, I predict their myths would explain storms, bad harvests, and why the weather changes."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"How do your predictions compare with a group that read a different text?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Our text was about thinkers, so we predicted myths about why the world exists. The group that read about the First Greeks focused on survival, like storms and crops. Both show that myths answer questions people could not answer yet."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Did the authors present ancient Greece in the same way? What did one text emphasize that another did not?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"The myth history text focused on stories and beliefs. The thinkers text focused on people asking questions and learning. They each show a different part of Greek life."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"note","text":"RI.6.7 is addressed lightly here: today's lesson is words only, so students integrate information from several text sources rather than images. Make clear that later lessons will add other media. For RI.6.9, listen for comparison of how each author focuses on a different aspect of the same world."},{"type":"pulse-check","standards":["RI.6.9"],"stem":"Two groups read different articles about ancient Greece. One article focuses on stories and gods, and the other on thinkers asking questions. What is the best way to compare them?","choices":[{"text":"They are about different places, so they cannot be compared.","correct":false,"rationale":"Both articles are about ancient Greece, so they can be compared."},{"text":"They present the same world, but each emphasizes a different part of Greek life, so together they give a fuller picture.","correct":true,"rationale":"This compares how each author presents the topic and what each emphasizes."},{"text":"The article about gods is true and the one about thinkers is made up.","correct":false,"rationale":"Both are informational texts and nothing says either is invented."},{"text":"They say exactly the same things in different words.","correct":false,"rationale":"The articles emphasize different ideas, so they do not repeat each other."}]},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Support students in sharing predictions and comparing across texts by using modal verb forms and by building on partners' ideas.","sayAsk":"Provide frames: 'I predict that myths would explain ___ because ___.' 'Our text says ___, but their text says ___.' 'I agree with ___, and I would add ___.' Model verbs for prediction: would explain, might show, could describe. Allow students to point at poster facts while speaking.","watchFor":"If students list facts without a prediction, then prompt: 'What would people want explained because of that fact?' If students use only simple present for predictions, then model 'would' or 'might'. Success: students state a prediction tied to a fact, use a modal verb, and respond to another group's idea."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: connecting facts to predictions","tryThis":"Give a bridge frame: 'If people depended on ___, they would be afraid of ___, so a myth might explain ___.' Work through one fact with the group."},{"situation":"Ready for extension: comparing across texts","tryThis":"Ask students to explain what a reader would miss if they read only one of the three texts, and to cite a fact from each."}]}]}]},{"kind":"look-back","title":"Look Back","purpose":"Students synthesize what they learned about the world that produces myths and reflect on how reading aloud with pauses helps comprehension.","activities":[{"id":"look-back-quick-write","title":"Quick Write: A World That Needs Stories","minutes":5,"standards":["RI.6.1","RI.6.9"],"routine":"Quick Write","blocks":[{"type":"directions","text":"Use the **Quick Write** routine. In 3-4 sentences, explain what you learned about ancient Greece from the texts and what myths you predict that world would create. Use at least one piece of evidence and one verb such as *shows*, *suggests*, or *explains*."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Based on the facts you read, what do you think people in ancient Greece needed their stories to do?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"The text shows that Greeks relied on the sea and farming and didn't have science to explain nature. I predict they needed stories to explain storms and keep them feeling safe. This suggests myths came from real needs, which helps me understand why a book like The Lightning Thief uses them."}]}]},{"kind":"homework","title":"Homework","purpose":"Optional independent practice.","activities":[{"id":"homework-reading-log","title":"Independent Reading and Reflection","minutes":0,"standards":[],"blocks":[{"type":"paragraph","audience":"shared","text":"Optional: Read your independent reading book for 20 minutes. Then reread aloud one paragraph from today's text, pausing where the meaning calls for it, and write one sentence about why the author paused and what idea is emphasized."}]}]}]},"digest":{"summary":"Students read teacher-selected paragraphs from three Newsela texts about ancient Greece, extract facts with evidence, use context clues and practice prosody with a metacognitive question about pauses. They then make prediction posters about what myths from such a world would explain and compare predictions across texts.","keyActivities":["Launch: recall Lesson 1 and model context clues and prosody","Part A: group reading aloud, fact extraction and evidence annotation","Part B: prediction posters and gallery walk comparing texts","Quick Write on what the world of ancient Greece needed its stories to do"],"vocabularyTaught":["context clue","predict","prosody","city-state","philosophy","myth"],"standardsCovered":["L.6.4.a","RI.6.1","RI.6.7","RI.6.9","SL.6.1","ELD.PI.6.1","ELD.PI.6.6","ELD.PII.6.3"]}}
